title: What Causes Musculoskeletal Pain?

items.text: Nociceptive — direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury
items.md: Nociceptive — direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury

items.text: Inflammatory — pain driven by inflammatory mediators
items.md: Inflammatory — pain driven by inflammatory mediators

items.text: Neuropathic — pain from nerve injury or dysfunction
items.md: Neuropathic — pain from nerve injury or dysfunction

items.text: Acute — recent onset, often tied to identifiable injury or flare
items.md: Acute — recent onset, often tied to identifiable injury or flare

items.text: Chronic — persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months
items.md: Chronic — persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months

items.text: Treatment approach differs sharply between the two
items.md: Treatment approach differs sharply between the two

notes: Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory — pure neuropathic pain is more the territory of a separate pharmacology unit.

title: Inflammation Drives Pain

items.text: Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.

emphasis.text: Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.

items.md: **Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**

notes: This mediator list is the roadmap for the whole lecture — NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

title: Acetaminophen

items.text: ●  Analgesic effect: relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.

emphasis.text: ●  Analgesic effect:

items.md: **●  Analgesic effect:** relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.

items.text: ●  Antipyretic effect: reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.

emphasis.text: ●  Antipyretic effect:

items.md: **●  Antipyretic effect:** reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.

items.text: ●  Anti-inflammatory effect: minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.

emphasis.text: ●  Anti-inflammatory effect:

items.md: **●  Anti-inflammatory effect:** minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.

notes: This is the single most important distinction students need: acetaminophen treats pain and fever well, but it is not an anti-inflammatory drug the way NSAIDs are.

title: Acetaminophen Toxicity

items.text: In overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows — this is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

emphasis.text: In overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows — this is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

items.md: **In overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows — this is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.**

notes: NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine. Tie this directly back to the "toxic metabolite" bullet from Lecture 1’s drug metabolism section.

title: The Hidden Acetaminophen Overdose

items.text: A patient takes acetaminophen regularly for chronic back pain. For a cold, they also start an over-the-counter combination cold-and-flu medication.
items.md: A patient takes acetaminophen regularly for chronic back pain. For a cold, they also start an over-the-counter combination cold-and-flu medication.

items.text: Ask yourself:  What is the hidden danger in this combination?

emphasis.text: Ask yourself:
What is the hidden danger in this combination?

items.md: **Ask yourself:** **What is the hidden danger in this combination?**

items.text: Clinical pearl:  Many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury. Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.

emphasis.text: Clinical pearl:

Many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury. Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.

items.md: **Clinical pearl:** **Many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury. Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.**

notes: Good moment to reinforce generic-name awareness from Lecture 1 — patients often do not realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label.

title: COX-1 vs. COX-2

items.text: Maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow
items.md: Maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow

items.text: Inhibition contributes to GI and renal adverse effects
items.md: Inhibition contributes to GI and renal adverse effects

items.text: Induced mainly at sites of inflammation
items.md: Induced mainly at sites of inflammation

items.text: Selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity
items.md: Selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity

notes: Stress this is a simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation — COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.

items.text: Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.

emphasis.text: Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.

items.md: **Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.**

items.text: Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain
items.md: Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain

items.text: Diclofenac — available in oral and topical formulations
items.md: Diclofenac — available in oral and topical formulations

items.text: Indomethacin — more potent, more GI/CNS adverse effects
items.md: Indomethacin — more potent, more GI/CNS adverse effects

items.text: Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk

emphasis.text: Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk

items.md: **Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk**

title: COX-2 Selective Inhibition: Celecoxib

items.text: Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.

emphasis.text: Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.

items.text: GI effects: lower risk of ulcer/bleeding than nonselective NSAIDs.
items.md: GI effects: lower risk of ulcer/bleeding than nonselective NSAIDs.

items.text: Cardiovascular risk: COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.

emphasis.text: Cardiovascular risk: COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.

items.md: **Cardiovascular risk: COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.**

items.text: Renal effects: similar renal risk to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.
items.md: Renal effects: similar renal risk to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.

notes: This is a classic "trade one risk for another" teaching point — better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.

title: NSAID Adverse Effects
tables: Decreased renal perfusion, fluid retention, acute kidney injury
Hypertension, increased risk of cardiovascular events
notes: These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion that follows. Table 1.

title: NSAID Contraindications & Interactions

items.text: Active GI bleeding or ulcer history
items.md: Active GI bleeding or ulcer history

items.text: NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk ("triple whammy" with diuretics)
items.md: NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk ("triple whammy" with diuretics)

items.text: NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk
items.md: NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk

notes: The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a very high-yield acute kidney injury pattern to flag explicitly.

title: Osteoarthritis vs. Rheumatoid Arthritis

items.text: Treatment goal: pain control and function
items.md: Treatment goal: pain control and function

items.text: Treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain
items.md: Treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain

notes: This distinction is the hinge the whole rest of the section turns on: OA is managed primarily with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.

items.text: Acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain
items.md: Acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain

items.text: Oral NSAIDs — effective, but carry the systemic risks already discussed
items.md: Oral NSAIDs — effective, but carry the systemic risks already discussed

items.text: Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure
items.md: Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure

items.text: Intra-articular corticosteroid injections — short-term relief for flares in a single joint
items.md: Intra-articular corticosteroid injections — short-term relief for flares in a single joint

items.text: Other approaches — activity modification, physical therapy, weight management

title: What Makes a Drug "Disease-Modifying"?

items.text: ●  DMARD: Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug — a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.

emphasis.text: ●  DMARD:

items.md: **●  DMARD:** Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug — a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.

items.text: ●  Goal of therapy: slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.

emphasis.text: ●  Goal of therapy:

items.md: **●  Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.

notes: Contrast explicitly with NSAIDs: an NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the underlying disease trajectory — a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.

items.text: Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens (next slide)

emphasis.text: Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens (next slide)

items.md: **Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens (next slide)**

items.text: Hydroxychloroquine — milder disease; relatively favorable safety profile
items.md: Hydroxychloroquine — milder disease; relatively favorable safety profile

items.text: Sulfasalazine — often used in combination regimens
items.md: Sulfasalazine — often used in combination regimens

items.text: Leflunomide — alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated
items.md: Leflunomide — alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated

title: Methotrexate

items.text: Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.

emphasis.text: Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.

items.md: **Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.**

items.text: Dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.

emphasis.text: Dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.

items.md: **Dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.**

items.text: Folate supplementation is routinely co-prescribed to reduce toxicity.
items.md: Folate supplementation is routinely co-prescribed to reduce toxicity.

items.text: Key adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity.
items.md: Key adverse effects: hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity.

emphasis.text: Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).

notes: Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety teaching points in all of rheumatology pharmacology — emphasize it strongly.
